intro.text: The Library holds every book in the city, but its card catalog is written in thousands of lines of C. The librarians want something shorter.
Quack. Python does the same jobs in far fewer lines. Let's write some real Python. It runs right here in your browser.

mid.text: The catalog code shrinks. But librarians keep tripping on habits carried over from C.
Quack. Some things look familiar and behave differently. Check yourself.

outro.text: Shelves sorted, catalog compact. The Library hums.
Quack. Next: Billboard Boulevard, where code becomes something people can see.

games.title: The Catalog Desk
games.instructions: Write the function, then run the hidden tests. First load of Python takes a few seconds. Tab indents.

tasks.prompt: Write shout(s): return s in capitals with an exclamation mark on the end.
tasks.hint: Strings have an .upper() method, and + joins strings.
tasks.solved: Strings are objects with methods. No malloc needed.

tasks.prompt: Write evens(nums): return a new list of only the even numbers.
tasks.hint: A list comprehension: [n for n in nums if ...]. Even means n % 2 == 0.
tasks.solved: One line replaces a C loop, a counter and an array.

tasks.prompt: Write count_words(text): return a dict mapping each word to how many times it appears.
tasks.hint: for w in text.split(): counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
tasks.solved: A dict is a hash table. Week 5's lockers, built in.

rounds.q: Which Python loop does the same as C's for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)?
In Python 3, what does 1 / 3 evaluate to?
rounds.explain: Python 3's / is true division. Use // for floor division. (Remember Week 1's integer-division bug?)

rounds.q: How does Python know where a block of code ends?
rounds.explain: Indentation is part of the syntax.

rounds.q: A C array has a fixed size. What is the closest Python type that can grow?
rounds.explain: A list can grow with append() and shrink with pop().
